question_text: A 50-year-old man comes to the emergency department for evaluation of right-sided facial weakness that he noticed after waking up. He took ibuprofen to relieve symptoms, which subsided a week later. He has a 5-year history of hypertension controlled with drug therapy. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years and he drinks two beers daily. His vital signs are within the normal range. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

                    ### Question
                    A 50-year-old man comes to the emergency department for evaluation of right-sided facial weakness that he noticed after waking up. One month ago, he also experienced right-sided neck pain and headache that began after returning from a hunting trip to New Hampshire the week before. He took ibuprofen to relieve symptoms, which subsided a week later. He has a 5-year history of hypertension controlled with drug therapy. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years and he drinks two beers daily. His vital signs are within the normal range. Physical examination shows right-sided drooping of the upper and lower half of the face. The patient has difficulties smiling and he is unable to close his right eye. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Western blot
opb. Polymerase chain reaction of the facial skin
opc. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis
opd. Enzyme‑linked immunosorbent assay
ope. Noncontrast CT

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with right-sided facial weakness, indicating a possible lower motor neuron lesion, which could be due to Bell's palsy or a stroke. The recent history of neck pain and headache, along with the hunting trip in New Hampshire, raises suspicion for Lyme disease, a tick-borne illness that can cause neurological symptoms. Given these considerations, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis is the most appropriate next step to confirm or rule out Lyme disease, as it can provide evidence of infection through the presence of antibodies or the organism itself. This aligns with the consensus that CSF analysis is critical in cases of suspected Lyme neuroborreliosis, especially with the patient's exposure history.
